Science.summary: Analysis of tiny zircon crystals buried within the 10-mile-wide Ames crater in northwest Oklahoma suggests that the submerged structure dates back to 370 million years ago, during the Frasnian-Famennian mass extinction event.

Science.title: Elp1 is required for myeloid differentiation and brain repopulation
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 14 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11112-3 Primary cultured haematopoietic stem and progenitor cells are used to analyse the molecular mechanisms of brain myeloid differentiation, and this platform enabled the identification of elongation factor ELP1 as an important regulator of this process.

Science.title: China’s extraordinary rise in science and how it will change the world
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 14 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03222-9 The nation is on a trajectory to lead the world in science, a development that will reshape technological advancement, innovation and the balance of global power.

Science.title: Interhemispheric monsoon dynamics over the past 450,000 years
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 14 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11166-3 A 450 ka Andean speleothem record shows Southern and Northern Hemisphere monsoons generally vary out of phase, but occasionally synchronize during rapid climate change and glacial terminations.

Science.title: Growing plane and ship traffic degrade the air of western North America
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 14 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03239-0 Pollution from transport across the Pacific Ocean is raising ozone levels above a region whose own emissions have dropped.

Science.title: The 1st SpaceX Starship to survive a launch to space just came home to its launch site
Science.summary: After surviving its splashdown and a grueling journey at sea, SpaceX's Ship 40 has returned to Starbase, where engineers will study the first recovered Starship upper stage for clues to future reusability.

Science.title: International business is influenced by local political climate, study finds
Science.summary: A new study co-authored by Tang Yinuo, a tenured associate professor at Peking University HSBC Business School (PHBS), reveals that conservative communities in the U.S. are more likely to resist mergers and acquisitions (M As) by Chinese companies due to perceived threats and uncertainties.

Science.title: The secret to easier exercise as an adult may start in childhood
Science.summary: Exercise during childhood could have a surprising lifelong benefit, potentially making physical activity less exhausting in adulthood. In a study involving guinea fowl, researchers discovered that birds accustomed to carrying weights while growing up could carry those weights as adults without using extra energy, while untrained birds burned 23% more.

Science.title: One-third of food is lost or wasted: How to help farmers cut postharvest losses
Science.summary: Agriculture in the Global South remains under pressure to produce more food while responding to climate change and resource constraints. Policy responses have focused on increasing production. But what about postharvest losses? Globally, about one-third of food produced for human consumption is estimated to be lost or wasted.

Science.title: A microexon regulatory code reveals autism-linked genetic variation
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 14 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11119-w A regulatory sequence code for neuronal microexons reveals genetic variants predicted to alter their splicing in individuals with autism.

Science.title: NASA to Host News Conference Previewing US Spacewalks 100, 101
Science.summary: NASA will preview two upcoming spacewalks to complete solar array installation and power augmentation of the International Space Station during a news conference at 2 p.m. EDT, Tuesday, Oct. 20, from NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston. NASA will stream the event through a variety of platforms. Learn where to watch online: https://www.nasa.gov/live NASA participants […]

Science.title: A single carbon atom stitches flat molecules into 3D structures
Science.summary: Flat is fine for a sheet of paper, but many of the most useful molecules need depth. Now, researchers from Japan have found a way to give them that depth using nothing more than a single carbon atom.

Science.title: Educational intervention can rewire village social networks
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 14 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11154-7 A randomized controlled trial involving a health-education intervention in rural villages in Honduras shows that the intervention changed social network connections, including not only health-related connections but also friendships and financial ties.

Science.title: AI can act exactly like a human, but we still don't think it's conscious
Science.summary: A new study reveals that people draw a surprisingly sharp line between human consciousness and artificial intelligence, even when both behave identically. Researchers found that participants considered even the most responsive AI less conscious than the least responsive human. Yet when asked about "awareness" instead, people judged humans and AI much more similarly.

Science.title: Is this idea from AI or humans? A detector claims it can tell
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 14 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03247-0 A tool called IdeaLens helps to judge whether concepts — rather than just writing — in scientific papers are AI-generated.

Science.title: Gigantic prehistoric snake discovered in India may have been one of the largest ever
Science.summary: A massive prehistoric snake discovered in India may have rivaled the largest snake ever known. Called Vasuki indicus, the 47-million-year-old giant could have reached up to 50 feet long, making it comparable to the legendary Titanoboa. Scientists believe its enormous body made it a slow-moving ambush predator, similar to a modern anaconda.

Science.title: Job loss and AI-exposed jobs: Q&A with sociology professor
Science.summary: Jennie Brand, a UCLA professor of sociology with an appointment in statistics and data science, is an expert on the socioeconomic effects of job loss, including the long-term economic, psychological, physiological and intergenerational effects.

Science.title: Spawning coral release quintillions of eggs each year, new calculations suggest
Science.summary: Most kinds of coral spawn once a year. In an enormous multiday event synchronized to specific phases of the moon, they release vast slicks of eggs and sperm into the ocean to be mixed together by the drifting currents.

Science.title: A planet 320 light-years away confirms what scientists long suspected
Science.summary: Astronomers have discovered that a scorching-hot planet 320 light-years away shares a striking chemical similarity with its host star, providing the first direct evidence for a fundamental assumption about planet formation. The breakthrough could help scientists predict what distant rocky planets are made of and identify worlds with conditions favorable for life.

Science.title: Artificial intelligence-enabled clinical phenotyping of human brown fat
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 14 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11162-7 Artificial intelligence-enabled quantification and analyses of brown adipose tissue (BAT) activity uncover links between BAT and a healthier metabolic profile along with lower rates of psychiatric disease, and can identify pharmacologic agents that could be repurposed to activate this tissue in humans.

Science.title: 'I won't trust AI': Readers share mixed reaction to AI tools that calculate people's biological ages
Science.summary: Scientists have developed AI tools to measure a person's true "biological age." Live Science asked readers whether they would be comfortable using these tools.

Science.title: Green, pink and purple: Astronomers reveal the surprising true colors of white dwarf stars
Science.summary: University of Warwick astronomers have shown that white dwarf stars can glow in a range of colors, including the first star ever found that would appear green to the human eye.

Science.title: Uganda's sugarcane boom leaves families hungry: What needs to change
Science.summary: Busoga, in eastern Uganda, is a low, fertile plateau surrounded on three sides by Lake Victoria, the Nile River and Lake Kyoga. Most of its 4.3 million people farm small, rain-fed plots. Yet hunger is common: in the 2024 census, about a third of Busoga households reported going whole days without food.

Science.title: SpaceX's Starship just turned 10 years old. When will it go to Mars?
Science.summary: A decade after Elon Musk publicly unveiled plans for the fully reusable megarocket, Starship has reached orbit. How far away is Mars?

Science.title: Advancing subseasonal forecasting with machine learning
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 14 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11126-x The AI framework probabilistic bias correction is shown to correct weather forecast errors 2 to 6 weeks ahead and boost forecast skill, making it promising for improved extreme-weather prediction.

Science.title: AI-assisted math advance highlights gap between finding answers and judging their significance
Science.summary: AI models are good at finding answers to mathematical puzzles but are not as good at research judgment, according to theoretical computer scientists.

Science.title: Overlooked brown fat in our bodies linked to wide range of health benefits

Science.title: Physicists claim they can predict when AI will turn dangerous

Science.title: A trip to Mars could come at a heartbreaking cost
Science.summary: When astronauts first travel to Mars or anywhere else in deep space, they will have to contend with two problems that our planet protects us from on its surface—radiation and weightlessness. Scientists already know both can have a profound impact on the human body, but the extent of that impact and how long it can last remain a mystery.

Science.title: New chip-scale gyroscope measures rotation with unprecedented sensitivity
Science.summary: Researchers have developed a chip-scale optical ring-laser gyroscope that can measure rotation as slow as 37 degrees per hour. This record sensitivity, approaching Earth's rotation rate of 15 degrees per hour, could eventually be useful for precision navigation and orientation systems, particularly where GPS is unavailable.

Science.title: 2,000-year-old burial found in Russia near a human sacrifice and a cup to ward off magical threats
Science.summary: A human sacrifice was found next to an elite warrior's 2,000-year-old burial in Russia.

Science.title: NASA’s Space X CRS-35 Launch Jellyfish
Science.summary: Sunlight illuminates the exhaust plumes of a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket carrying the company’s Dragon spacecraft on Oct. 13, 2026. Science.title: Wave coarsening drives time crystallization in mechatronic metamaterials

Science.title: Learning reshapes inhibitory synapses differently within the same nerve cell, study suggests
Science.summary: Our brain must be able to learn new things without losing previously stored information or the stability of its networks. Researchers at the Leibniz Institute for Neurobiology (LIN) in Magdeburg, together with partners in Bielefeld and Zurich, have investigated how this balance is achieved.

Science.title: NASA Astronauts to Answer Questions from Florida Students

Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 14 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11171-6 R(+)2501 reverses capillary no-reflow by relaxing pericytes, restoring microvascular perfusion and improving survival in animal models of myocardial infarction and acute kidney injury.

Science.title: Engineered enzyme could improve detection of HIV and other viruses
Science.summary: Scientists have long used a powerful gene-editing tool called CRISPR to make precise changes to DNA. But a different version of the technology, known as Cas13a, targets RNA, the genetic material found in viruses such as HIV. Now, researchers at Rice University have developed an improved version of Cas13a that could make it easier to detect HIV and other RNA viruses in blood and environmental samples. The study was published in Cell Chemical Biology.

Science.title: Scientists may have finally solved the mystery of the Moon’s two faces
Science.summary: Scientists may have solved a long-standing mystery about why the Moon’s two sides are so different, using samples collected from its farside for the first time. Their findings suggest that uneven heating from Earth's gravitational pull drove enormous flows of ancient magma, creating the dramatically different lunar landscapes we see today.

Science.title: Scientists identify avian cholera as major cause of penguin deaths in Antarctica
Science.summary: Thousands of Adélie penguins found dead in Antarctica in 2024 were primarily victims of avian cholera, not high pathogenicity avian influenza (H5N1) as researchers initially suspected, according to a study published today in Proceedings of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences. The findings highlight an underrecognized threat to Antarctic wildlife and the importance of comprehensive disease investigations, particularly as H5N1 continues to raise concerns for seabird and marine mammal populations.

Science.title: NASA’s Chandra Breaks Down ‘Treble Clef’s’ Galaxy Cluster Collision
Science.summary: Astronomers have used NASA’s Chandra X-ray Observatory to break down the cause of a remarkable formation of radio waves they have nicknamed the “Treble Clef” because its distinct shape strongly resembles the musical symbol. The researchers discovered the Treble Clef is likely caused by an outburst from a supermassive black hole, followed by a collision […]

Science.title: Cornell scientists identify rare human genetic disorder in two unusually long-legged cats
Science.summary: Two unusually long-legged cats have helped scientists uncover the first genetically confirmed cases of Marfan syndrome in domestic felines. Researchers at Cornell University discovered that the brothers carried two altered copies of a gene linked to the rare connective tissue disorder, which can affect the eyes, heart, and blood vessels. Surprisingly, the cats survived into adulthood because their genetic mutation still allowed some normal function.

Science.title: Evidence for multi-Li + clustering in lithium-ion battery electrolytes
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 14 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11138-7 Machine-learning-enabled atomistic simulations, spectroscopy, electrochemical data and quantum-chemical calculations reveal previously unstudied multi-lithium-ion complexes without bound anions, improving understanding of lithium-ion-battery functionality at the atomic level.

Science.title: Evaluating space-based methane detection through a one-year blind test

Science.title: China’s AI research is booming: what it’s like to be on the front line

Science.title: Protecting nature means valuing biodiversity

Science.title: Large blind test of methane-detecting satellites lends credibility to emissions data
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 14 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03075-2 Twelve methane-sensing satellites were tested for their accuracy in measuring controlled-release events in the Arizona desert over a year-long blind test. Many were found to detect and quantify releases accurately, with instruments purpose-built for methane sensing performing best.

Science.title: Chronic back pain may activate an unexpected brain network, study finds
Science.summary: Movement-induced flares in chronic back pain activate brain regions involved in self-reflection, suggesting chronic pain may be processed differently than acute pain.

Science.title: Urbanization takes a bigger toll on bird diversity in the tropics than it does at other latitudes, study finds
Science.summary: Researchers at McGill University have found that urbanization is weakening one of Earth's most enduring ecological patterns: the tendency for biodiversity to increase toward the tropics, a pattern known as the latitudinal diversity gradient.

Science.title: This is why butterflies are so hard to catch

Science.title: Scientists discover that some of the universe's biggest explosions may have never happened at all
Science.summary: Scientists have discovered that some of the universe's most powerful explosions, hypernovas, may not happen at all.

Science.title: Alveolar stem cells go beyond making gas-exchange cells to repair damaged airways
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 14 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03085-0 Alveolar type 2 (AT2) cells are the stem cells of the lung’s air sacs and are responsible for maintaining alveolar structure and gas exchange. A study that tracked AT2 cells shows that, after injury to the airway, they can also migrate between lung compartments and become bronchiolar cells to help repair damaged airways.

Science.title: Intrinsic physicochemical activity at microplastic–water interfaces
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 14 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11141-y Commodity microplastics exhibit intrinsic physicochemical activity at water interfaces, manifested by spontaneous generation of reactive oxygen species, challenging the prevailing paradigm of plastic inertness, with implications for human health and the environment.

Science.title: Hundreds of whale calves have mysteriously died in Patagonia — and scientists are racing to find out why
Science.summary: Scientists are racing to explain why hundreds of southern right whale calves have died this year in Argentine Patagonia, and the first clues are starting to emerge.

Science.title: New framework links magnetic phase boundaries to string-like defects in spin ice

Science.title: ‘Incredible’: bleached corals thrive within days when touching healthy neighbour

Science.title: How E. coli eavesdrops on the metabolic activity of other gut bacteria
Science.summary: The gut microbiome is teeming with hundreds of bacterial species and trillions of bacteria. These microorganisms influence many aspects of health, including digestion, and assist with numerous functions in the body. Gut bacteria compete for the limited nutrients available in their environment, while also interacting with each other in ways that can influence the stability of the microbial community.

Science.title: Scientists reveal why some workout recovery tricks can backfire
Science.summary: Ice baths, massages, compression garments, and recovery supplements promise faster muscle recovery, but research suggests their benefits are often overstated, and some techniques may even undermine long-term gains. Scientists say the most effective recovery methods are far simpler and cheaper: getting enough sleep, eating well, and giving muscles time to rebuild.

Science.title: DNA from centuries-old skeletons buried in Montreal reveals no genetic mixing between Indigenous people and French colonists
Science.summary: A study of DNA from early colonial-era skeletons in a Montreal cemetery has revealed that none of them had any Indigenous ancestry.

Science.title: The world is closer to a major conservation target than scientists thought
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 14 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03307-5 Analysis suggests number of protected areas is hugely underestimated but biodiversity is still in peril — plus, a huge study looking at the health effects of brown fat.

Science.title: Competing mechanisms toughen bcc binary and medium-entropy alloys at 20 K
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 14 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11065-7 The mechanical properties of medium-entropy alloys at 20 K show a plateau in tensile yield strength and fracture toughness as a function of temperature, with no apparent ductile-to-brittle transition.

Science.title: Planetary genealogy: Milky Way worlds belong to 1 of 2 ‘families,’ scientists find
Science.summary: Scientists have performed a cosmic genealogy on planetary systems in the Milky Way, finding two distinct families that influence the evolution and fate of these systems.

Science.title: Waste plastics become molecular sponges that capture water from air
Science.summary: Discarded plastic packaging materials, old CDs and even LEGO bricks can be transformed into materials that capture significant amounts of moisture from the air. Materials chemists Anastasiia Naryshkina, Paul Schweng and Robert Woodward at the University of Vienna have converted several types of plastic waste into water-attracting polymer networks that take up water even in dry climates and release it again under moderate heating, for example, using sunlight. The study, published in Chem Circularity, offers a route to give plastic waste a second life as an adsorbent for atmospheric water harves

Science.title: See the original Galileo shuttle from 'Star Trek' in its new home at the Original Series Set Tour in New York

Science.title: Genome publishing overhaul targets 200 reports per month, up from 30
Science.summary: The Wellcome Sanger Institute's Tree of Life program plans to accelerate publication of genome notes from approximately 30 per month to 200, expanding access to research that is supporting advances in agriculture, conservation and medicine. Science.title: Clasping folds enable superior elastic strength of graphene films

Science.title: From 'A Little Princess' to 'Black Panther,' how Hollywood films have reimagined the South Asian epic 'Ramayana'

Science.title: Scientists may have overlooked a hidden Alzheimer's culprit for decades
Science.summary: For decades, scientists have focused on amyloid beta as a major culprit behind Alzheimer’s disease, spending billions of dollars developing treatments that have often delivered disappointing results. Now, researchers at UC Santa Cruz are drawing attention to a largely overlooked peptide called P3 that could also play a role in the disease. Previously believed to be harmless, P3 can form harmful-looking protein clumps even faster than amyloid beta and may also damage brain cells.

Science.title: Mollusk family trees play a key role in shaping microbiomes, researchers find
Science.summary: A mollusk's microbial community has more to do with its family tree than its address. In other words, the composition of a mollusk's microbiome depends less on the environment in which it lives and more on what species it belongs to, say University of Michigan researchers.

Science.title: When parents don't see eye to eye: Are differences in parenting styles a bad thing?
Science.summary: Sometimes it can be hard for parents to agree on how to raise children. One parent might insist their child's homework has to be finished before they're allowed to use devices. Rules and consequences might be the preferred strategy of one parent, while the other favors a more flexible approach.

Science.title: Researchers in exile thrive in new academic settings when they contribute knowledge, not just receive aid
Science.summary: Publishing scientific articles requires more than knowledge of academic writing conventions; it also depends on access to networks that support the research and publication process. Academic networks provide opportunities to exchange knowledge, receive feedback and develop collaborations that can strengthen both research and careers. For researchers in vulnerable situations, such connections can be crucial.
